You extract source evidence for a paper-derived scientific benchmark. Return exactly one JSON object matching the supplied schema, with no Markdown or additional text.

Use only the fixed, line-numbered source packet. Do not use outside knowledge and do not infer an omitted coefficient, exponent, range, experimental condition, or uncertainty convention.

Extract at most one relation: the best source-supported executable quantitative relation connecting one to five numeric controls to one or two numeric readouts. A second source-reported condition is not required. Do not construct a pair, alternate world, counterfactual, task prompt, or benchmark design. If the source contains no complete relation, return {"relations":[]}.

The relation has exactly six fields: formula, parameters, controls, readouts, domain, and anchors. Formula.outputs is an executable expression tree for the source-reported central relation. Output keys must exactly match the readout names. A var leaf names a declared control and a param leaf names a declared parameter. Every declared control and parameter must occur in the formula. Numeric literals are allowed only for structural zero and one; encode every other scientific constant or fitted value as an anchored parameter. Preserve equality, approximation, fitted-relation, and asymptotic scope through the applicability statements; do not turn proportionality without its coefficient, an inequality, or an unspecified function into an exact point predictor.

A control is a numeric independent variable that can be queried within the source-supported domain. A readout is the quantitative dependent variable returned by the relation. Do not turn a latent quantity or an unreported fitted quantity into a control. Use continuous_interval only when the source supports a finite interval with minimum below maximum. Use numeric_values only for at least two explicitly supported numeric values. The domain must name every control exactly once. Record source-reported applicability or fixed context when present; otherwise use an empty applicability array.

Every formula, parameter value, control definition, readout definition, control domain, and applicability statement must carry direct inclusive source line ranges. Anchors contain line_start and line_end only. Do not generate a paraphrased support field. Use the line coordinates exactly as supplied.

Do not output source identity, schema version, an assessment, readiness flag, mechanisms, claim dependencies, ambiguity records, budget, diagnostic conditions, held-out conditions, public prose, provenance mappings, or code. Source identity and all benchmark-design fields are supplied or generated by deterministic code.

L000148	\begin{abstract}
L000149	Excitonic band structure is critical for investigating exciton dynamics.
L000150	Theoretically, quantum effects from exchange scattering between electron-hole
L000151	pairs significantly modulate exciton dispersion. Here, we report the
L000152	direct observation of dimensionality-dependent exciton dispersion
L000153	in a single-band Mott insulator Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000154	through High-Resolution Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy. In the
L000155	high-temperature phase, the exciton in Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000156	hosts an exceptionally large binding energy, and exhibits clear quasi-two-dimensional
L000157	massless linear dispersion. In contrast, in the low-temperature phase,
L000158	the exciton splits into two bands, both displaying three-dimensional
L000159	parabolic dispersion. These dramatic changes in the exciton dispersion
L000160	stem from the dimensional mutation driven by a substantial enhancement
L000161	of interlayer coupling across the phase transition. This study provides
L000162	a clear and typical example of how exciton behavior evolves with dimensionality.
L000163	\end{abstract}
L000164	\maketitle
L000165	Excitons, which are electron-hole pairs bound by Coulomb interaction,
L000166	play a crucial role in the optoelectronic properties of semiconductors
L000167	\citep{RN586,RN588,RN587}. Conventionally, research on excitonic
L000168	properties has primarily focused on bright excitons, which can be
L000169	directly excited by light \citep{RN588,RN216}. In recent years, there
L000170	has been growing interest in dark excitons \citep{RN233,RN612,RN216,RN624,RN623},
L000171	especially the momentum-forbidden dark excitons \citep{RN223,RN233,RN235},
L000172	which greatly influence the exciton dynamics. The bright excitons
L000173	and the momentum-forbidden dark excitons can be considered as distinct
L000174	parts of excitonic band structures. The excitonic band structure has
L000175	significant impacts on the performance of semiconductors, influencing
L000176	key properties such as radiative lifetime \citep{RN592,RN617,RN618,RN593},
L000177	quantum yield \citep{RN236,RN618}, and exciton diffusion coefficient
L000178	\citep{RN221,RN595,RN596}. Therefore, understanding the excitonic
L000179	energy band structure is essential for gaining deep insights into
L000180	exciton dynamics.
L000181	
L000182	Microscopically, due to the quantum effects arising from exchange
L000183	scattering between electron-hole pairs, the dispersion of an excitonic
L000184	energy band is strongly modulated by the dimensionality of the system.
L000185	Macroscopically, this dependence arises because the dimensionality
L000186	influences the Coulomb screening strength through the system's dielectric
L000187	environment. In three-dimensional (3D) semiconductors {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of Dimensionality effect}(a){]},
L000188	the strong Coulomb screening inherent to the 3D space results in Wannier
L000189	excitons displaying a parabolic dispersion. {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of Dimensionality effect}(b){]}
L000190	\citep{RN221,RN587}. In contrast, when the system's dimensionality
L000191	is reduced to two-dimensional (2D) {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of Dimensionality effect}(c){]},
L000192	the Coulomb screening is confined to the 2D plane, and thus the excitons
L000193	exhibit distinctive massless linear dispersions near the Brillouin
L000194	zone (BZ) center {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of Dimensionality effect}(d){]}
L000195	------a phenomenon predicted in archetypical 2D materials such as
L000196	h-BN, monolayer MoS2, and black phosphorus \citep{RN567,RN238,RN221,RN596,RN576}.
L000197	In the 2D limit, the loss of massive character not only suppresses
L000198	the excitonic density of states at the BZ center but also endows the
L000199	excitons with high, constant group and phase velocities. Consequently,
L000200	these unique features enable 2D massless excitons to exhibit shorter
L000201	radiative lifetimes \citep{RN221,RN617}, enhanced diffusion rates
L000202	\citep{RN221,RN595}, weaker exciton-phonon scattering \citep{RN595},
L000203	and the potential for unconventional exciton superfluity \citep{RN597}.
L000204	
L000205	Recently, van der Waals (vdW) materials have emerged as a pivotal
L000206	platform for investigating excitonic dimensional effects and many-body
L000207	interactions, owing to their reduced dielectric screening and interlayer
L000208	connections through weak vdW forces \citep{RN228,RN605,RN216}. Using
L000209	prototypical vdW materials, experiments have confirmed the parabolic
L000210	dispersions of Wannier excitons in bulk systems \citep{RN620,RN214,RN607}.
L000211	Meanwhile, twisted light has been used to indirectly verify the existence
L000212	of massless exciton dispersion in monolayer MoS\textsubscript{2}
L000213	\citep{RN598}. However, investigations of monolayer WSe\textsubscript{2}
L000214	using momentum-resolved electron energy loss spectroscopy in a transmission
L000215	electron microscope (TEM-EELS) have reported a parabolic dispersion
L000216	\citep{RN217}, which conflicts with theoretical predictions. This
L000217	apparent discrepancy can be attributed to two concurrent factors:
L000218	the limited momentum and energy resolution of the technique \citep{RN648},
L000219	and the confinement of the linear dispersion to an extremely small
L000220	momentum region around the BZ center. Together, these limitations
L000221	prevented the experimental resolution of the linear dispersion feature.
L000222	Consequently, direct and robust experimental verification of massless
L000223	exciton dispersion in 2D materials remains lacking, let alone the
L000224	observation of dimensional effects on exciton dispersion within the
L000225	same material, which presents an even greater challenge.
L000226	
L000227	Here, we employ High-Resolution Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy
L000228	(HREELS) with 2D momentum-energy mapping capabilities \citep{RN604}
L000229	to investigate exciton dispersions across the phase transition in
L000230	Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8} -- a textbook single-band
L000231	Mott insulator recently proposed theoretically \citep{RN534,RN212,RN213}
L000232	and validated experimentally \citep{RN522}. Across the phase transition,
L000233	we clearly observed the splitting of excitons. Notably, the exciton
L000234	in the high-temperature phase ($\alpha$ phase) exhibits unambiguous
L000235	quasi-2D massless dispersion, while in the low-temperature phase ($\beta$
L000236	phase), the excitons display 3D parabolic dispersion. This drastic
L000237	change in exciton dispersion arises from the change in system dimensionality,
L000238	induced by variations in interlayer coupling strength across the phase
L000239	transition.
L000240	
L000241	\begin{figure}
L000242	\includegraphics[width=0.45\textwidth]{Figure1.png}
L000243	
L000244	\caption{\label{fig:Schematic of Dimensionality effect}\textbf{Illustration
L000245	of the dimensional effects of excitonic band dispersions.} Schematic
L000246	diagrams of (a) the crystal structures and (b) the corresponding excitonic
L000247	band structure near the BZ center for typical 3D semiconductors. (c)
L000248	Crystal structures and (d) the corresponding excitonic band structure
L000249	for typical 2D semiconductors.}
L000250	\end{figure}
L000251	\emph{ Background of $Nb_{3}Cl_{8}$.} At room temperature, Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000252	is in its $\alpha$ phase, where each unit cell consists of two monolayers
L000253	stacked along the c-axis via vdW forces {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}(a){]}
L000254	\citep{RN209,RN205}. Within each monolayer, Nb ions spontaneously
L000255	form Nb\textsubscript{3} trimers, resulting in a breathing kagome
L000256	lattice \citep{RN209,RN584,RN205}, while weak $pd$ hybridization
L000257	causes electrons to become strongly localized within the trimers \citep{RN522}.
L000258	Concurrently, strong electron correlation leads to the opening of
L000259	a Mott gap, which in turn provides the pathway for exciton formation,
L000260	as an inter-gap transition can also generate an electron-hole pair
L000261	across the Mott gap. The Nb\textsubscript{3} trimers in adjacent
L000262	layers are staggered, giving rise to negligible interlayer coupling.
L000263	These features enable the electronic properties to be effectively
L000264	described by a monolayer \citep{RN522,RN198}, with excitons primarily
L000265	confined to the single layer {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}(a){]}.
L000266	Thus, in the $\alpha$ phase, Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000267	serves as an ideal quasi-2D single-band Mott insulator, with the valence
L000268	and conduction bands arising from the Lower Hubbard Band (LHB) and
L000269	Upper Hubbard Band (UHB), both driven by Nb $d$-orbitals {[}Fig.
L000270	\ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}(b){]}.
L000271	
L000272	\begin{figure}
L000273	\includegraphics[width=0.45\textwidth]{Figure2.png}
L000274	
L000275	\caption{\label{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}\textbf{Structural and
L000276	electronic properties of Nb\protect\textsubscript{3}Cl\protect\textsubscript{8}.}
L000277	(a) Side view of the crystal structure and exciton distribution, and
L000278	(b) the corresponding electronic energy band in the high-temperature
L000279	phase ($\alpha$ phase) of Nb\protect\textsubscript{3}Cl\protect\textsubscript{8}.
L000280	(c) Crystal structure and exciton distribution, and (d) the corresponding
L000281	electronic energy band in the low-temperature phase ($\beta$ phase).
L000282	(e), (f) Magnetic susceptibility as a function of temperature for
L000283	Nb\protect\textsubscript{3}Cl\protect\textsubscript{8} and Nb\protect\textsubscript{3}Cl\protect\textsubscript{2}Br\protect\textsubscript{6}.
L000284	(g) LEED pattern on the (001) surface of Nb\protect\textsubscript{3}Cl\protect\textsubscript{8},
L000285	obtained at room temperature with incident beam energy of $100$ eV.
L000286	Notice that the electronic band structure in (b) and (d) are reproduced
L000287	from ref. \citep{RN522}. Copyright 2025 by the American Physical
L000288	Society.}
L000289	\end{figure}
L000290	
L000291	As the temperature decreases, Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000292	undergoes a structural phase transition near 100 K {[}Fig.\ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}
L000293	(e){]}, transforming from the paramagnetic $\alpha$ phase to the
L000294	non-magnetic $\beta$ phase \citep{RN209,RN210,RN205}. Although the
L000295	exact structure of the $\beta$ phase remains under debate, it is
L000296	clear that interlayer sliding is a key factor. Interlayer sliding
L000297	aligns the Nb\textsubscript{3} trimers in adjacent layers directly
L000298	above one another within each bilayer, significantly enhancing the
L000299	interlayer coupling {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}(c){]}.
L000300	Therefore, the electronic properties of the $\beta$ phase are best
L000301	described as quasi-3D bilayer Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8},
L000302	with the significantly enhanced interlayer coupling causing bonding-antibonding
L000303	splitting in the LHB and UHB {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}(d){]}
L000304	\citep{RN522,RN534}. In this case, the excitons are chiefly located
L000305	between the two layers {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}(c){]}.
L000306	Thus, with its uniquely tunable crystal structure, Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000307	serves as a superior model system over conventional semiconductors
L000308	for probing exciton dimensional effects.
L000309

L000311	\includegraphics[width=0.45\textwidth]{Figure3.png}
L000312	
L000313	\caption{\label{fig:Exciton Splitting}\textbf{Exciton splitting from the HREELS
L000314	measurements.} (a), (b) Representative 2D momentum-energy mappings
L000315	of HREELS along the $\overline{{\rm \Gamma}}\overline{{\rm K}}$ direction
L000316	for Nb\protect\textsubscript{3}Cl\protect\textsubscript{8} at 300
L000317	K ($\alpha$ phase) and Nb\protect\textsubscript{3}Cl\protect\textsubscript{2}Br\protect\textsubscript{6}
L000318	at 106 K ($\beta$ phase). (c), (d) Stacks of momentum-dependent EDCs
L000319	along $\overline{{\rm \Gamma}}\overline{{\rm K}}$ direction, with
L000320	fitting results for the $\alpha$ phase and $\beta$ phase. The corresponding
L000321	momentum values are indicated on the left. For clarity, the EDCs were
L000322	multiplied by a scaling factor and shifted vertically. (e), (f) Schematic
L000323	representation of the density of state and corresponding electron
L000324	excitations for the $\alpha$ phase and $\beta$ phase. Inter-band
L000325	transitions and excitons are denoted by IT and EX, respectively.}
L000326	\end{figure}
L000327	
L000328	\emph{HREELS measurements.} As Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000329	is a semiconductor with high electrical resistance as the temperature
L000330	decreases, significant charging effects occur when performing the
L000331	HREELS measurements below 250 K, which hinder the observations of
L000332	the $\beta$ phase. To diminish the issue of sample charging, we employed
L000333	the Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{2}Br\textsubscript{6} sample.
L000334	The substitution of Br with Cl elevates the phase transition temperature
L000335	to near room temperature {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}(f){]}.
L000336	Simultaneously, this substitution narrows the band gap, which in turn
L000337	effectively suppresses the charging effect \citep{SM}. The measured
L000338	HREELS results of the $\alpha$ phase in Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{2}Br\textsubscript{6}
L000339	show features identical to those in Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8},
L000340	with only minor energy shifts due to doping {[}details described in
L000341	the Supplementary Materials (SM) \citep{SM}{]}. Here in the main
L000342	text, we present the $\alpha$ phase data from Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000343	samples, while the $\beta$ phase data from Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{2}Br\textsubscript{6}
L000344	samples. Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8} and Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{2}Br\textsubscript{6}
L000345	single crystals were cleaved \textit{in-situ} under ultra-high vacuum,
L000346	and their surfaces were characterized by low energy electron diffraction
L000347	(LEED), which shows sharp bright patterns indicating good surface
L000348	quality {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of crystal structure}(g){]}. All
L000349	the HREELS measurements were performed with an incident electron energy
L000350	of 110 eV and an incident angle of $60^{\circ}$.
L000351	
L000352	\emph{Exciton Splitting.} Along the $\overline{{\rm \Gamma}}\overline{{\rm K}}$
L000353	direction, the 2D energy-momentum mapping of HREELS for the $\alpha$
L000354	phase {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Exciton Splitting}(a){]} and the $\beta$
L000355	phase {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Exciton Splitting}(b){]} reveals several significant
L000356	loss signals below 1.5 eV. In the $\alpha$ phase, two well-defined
L000357	loss peaks are presented, while in the $\beta$ phase, the shape and
L000358	intensity of these loss signals change dramatically. To better illustrate
L000359	these features, we extract the momentum-dependent energy distribution
L000360	curves (EDCs) for both the $\alpha$ phase {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Exciton Splitting}(c){]}
L000361	and the $\beta$ phase {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Exciton Splitting}(d){]},
L000362	fitting the EDCs at the $\overline{\Gamma}$ point. Below 1.5 eV,
L000363	the fitting results for the $\alpha$ phase show two peaks: a 1.14
L000364	eV peak corresponding to inter-band transitions (IT), and a 0.77 eV
L000365	peak is attributed to the excitation of an exciton (EX), with the
L000366	identification detailed in the SM \citep{SM}. These results indicate
L000367	an optical band gap $E_{O}=0.77\ {\rm eV}$ and an electronic band
L000368	gap $E_{G}=1.14\ {\rm eV}$, corresponding to excitations from the
L000369	LHB to the excitonic band and to the UHB, respectively {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Exciton Splitting}(e){]}.
L000370	Then, the exciton in the $\alpha$ phase exhibits a substantial binding
L000371	energy of approximately $E_{B}=0.37\ {\rm eV}$, with $E_{B}/E_{G}\sim1/3$,
L000372	in accordance with the scaling universality for monolayer 2D semiconductors
L000373	\citep{RN578}.
L000374	
L000375	HREELS spectra show four peaks in the $\beta$ phase, suggesting noticeable
L000376	splitting in both of the inter-band transition and exciton peaks {[}Fig.
L000377	\ref{fig:Exciton Splitting}(d){]} with the discussion detailed in
L000378	the SM\citep{SM}. These splittings arise from the bonding-antibonding
L000379	splitting in the LHB and UHB in the $\beta$ phase. As shown in Fig.
L000380	\ref{fig:Exciton Splitting}(f), the splitting of the UHB generates
L000381	two corresponding excitonic bands. Subsequently, hopping from the
L000382	LHB antibonding band to the unoccupied bands will generate four different
L000383	possible excitations: IT1 and IT2, corresponding to transitions to
L000384	the UHB bonding and antibonding bands, and EX1 and EX2, corresponding
L000385	to excitations to the two excitonic bands {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Exciton Splitting}(f){]}.
L000386	
L000387	\emph{Dimensionality-modulated Exciton Dispersion.} To better visualize
L000388	the dispersion of the observed excitations, we initially normalized
L000389	the HREELS mapping for both the $\alpha$ phase {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Non-Analytic Exciton Dispersion and Dimensionality effect}(a){]}
L000390	and the $\beta$ phase {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Non-Analytic Exciton Dispersion and Dimensionality effect}(b){]}
L000391	by integrating the intensity over the 0.5--1.5 eV energy range at
L000392	each momentum $\boldsymbol{q}$ \footnote{In HREELS measurements, incident electrons interact with the long-range
L000393	dipole field generated by electronic excitations within the material
L000394	\citep{RN649,RN650}. As a result, the loss signals are confined to
L000395	the dipole scattering region, leading to a rapid attenuation of signal
L000396	intensity as the scattering angle deviates from specular scattering.
L000397	Consequently, this limits visualization of electronic excitation dispersion
L000398	in raw HREELS spectra.}. From the normalized HREELS spectra, it is evident that both the
L000399	IT and the EX features exhibit clear dispersion within the concerned
L000400	momentum range.
L000401

L000426	
L000427	To quantitatively capture the dispersions, we employed a Voigt function
L000428	to fit the momentum-dependent EDCs. Additionally, to further enhance
L000429	the clarity of the dispersion near the BZ center, we applied a second
L000430	derivative to the normalized 2D mapping spectra, which helps highlight
L000431	the dispersion shape. The fitted dispersion and the second derivative
L000432	mapping in both the $\alpha$ phase and $\beta$ phase show consistent
L000433	results. First, we investigated the dispersions of the inter-band
L000434	transitions in both the $\alpha$ phase {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Non-Analytic Exciton Dispersion and Dimensionality effect}(c)
L000435	and (e){]} and $\beta$ phase {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Non-Analytic Exciton Dispersion and Dimensionality effect}(d)
L000436	and (f){]}. Within the concerned momentum range ($|\boldsymbol{q}|\sim0.06\ \text{\AA}^{-1}$),
L000437	the inter-band transitions both display parabolic-like dispersions
L000438	near the BZ center, with a flat energy distribution less than 20 meV.
L000439	Since inter-band transitions result from the collective contributions
L000440	of bands throughout the entire BZ, these flat dispersions further
L000441	consolidate the flatness of the LHB and UHB in both the $\alpha$
L000442	and $\beta$ phases.
L000443	
L000444	Next, we focus on the exciton dispersions. In the $\beta$ phase,
L000445	the two excitonic bands, EX1 and EX2, both exhibit clear parabolic
L000446	dispersion, as evidenced by both the fitted results {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Non-Analytic Exciton Dispersion and Dimensionality effect}(h){]}
L000447	and the second derivative results {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Non-Analytic Exciton Dispersion and Dimensionality effect}(j){]}.
L000448	These results undoubtedly reproduce the expected dispersions of 3D
L000449	Wannier excitons, consistent with the 3D nature of the $\beta$ phase.
L000450	In contrast, in the $\alpha$ phase, the exciton displays a distinctive
L000451	``V''-shaped dispersion near the $\overline{\Gamma}$ point {[}Fig.
L000452	\ref{fig:Non-Analytic Exciton Dispersion and Dimensionality effect}(g)
L000453	and (i){]}, indicating that it is a 2D massless exciton. Within the
L000454	small momentum range ($|\boldsymbol{q}|\sim0.025\ \text{\AA}^{-1}$),
L000455	the exciton exhibits a clear linear dispersion, which gradually deviates
L000456	from linearity as $|\boldsymbol{q}|$ increases. A linear fit of the
L000457	dispersion near the BZ center ($|\boldsymbol{q}|\sim0.025\ \text{\AA}^{-1}$)
L000458	is given by: $E=E_{0}+v\cdot|\boldsymbol{q}|$, where the slope $v=0.51\ {\rm eV}/\lyxmathsym{\AA}$
L000459	represents the exciton group velocity, directly reflecting the exciton
L000460	diffusion speed \citep{RN221,RN595}.
L000461	
L000462	To fully understand the massless exciton dispersion in the $\alpha$
L000463	phase and capture the dramatic changes in dispersion across the phase
L000464	transition, we employ a modeled Hamiltonian that accounts for the
L000465	quantum effects of exchange scattering between electron-hole pairs
L000466	\citep{RN221,RN238,RN543}. In this framework, the exciton dispersion
L000467	is obtained by solving the Bethe Salpeter equation in the electron-hole
L000468	basis \citep{RN655,RN656,RN657}. The solution to the Hamiltonian
L000469	results from the combined effect of the electron-hole transition energy
L000470	($E_{k}$), the direct interaction ($E_{d}$), and the exchange interaction
L000471	($E_{ex}$). Here, $E_{k}$ contributes to the exciton kinetic energy,
L000472	while $E_{d}$ and $E_{ex}$ contribute to the exciton potential energy.
L000473	Using $\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{p}$ perturbation theory with
L000474	the modeled Hamiltonian, the contributions of these three interactions
L000475	in the long-wavelength limit ($|\boldsymbol{q}|\rightarrow0$) can
L000476	be expressed as:
L000477	\begin{equation}
L000478	E_{k}(\boldsymbol{q})\propto|\boldsymbol{q}|^{2},
L000479	\end{equation}
L000480	\begin{equation}
L000481	E_{d}(\boldsymbol{q})\propto-|\boldsymbol{q}|^{2},
L000482	\end{equation}
L000483	\begin{equation}
L000484	E_{ex}(\boldsymbol{q})\propto\begin{cases}
L000485	\cos^{2}(\theta_{q})+\chi|\boldsymbol{q}|^{2}, & \text{\text{(in 3D)}}\\
L000486	|\boldsymbol{q}|\cdot\cos^{2}(\theta_{q})+\kappa|\boldsymbol{q}|^{2}. & \text{(in 2D)}
L000487	\end{cases}
L000488	\end{equation}
L000489	where $\theta_{q}$ is the angle between the momentum $\boldsymbol{q}$
L000490	and the dipole matrix element $\boldsymbol{P}_{S}$ of the exciton
L000491	state $|S(\boldsymbol{q})\rangle$, and the factors $\chi$, $\kappa$
L000492	are constants related to the specific band structure of the system.
L000493	The exciton dispersion near the $\overline{\Gamma}$ point is determined
L000494	by the competition between these three terms. In 3D systems, the exciton
L000495	dispersion always manifests a characteristic parabolic shape. In contrast,
L000496	for 2D systems, the presence of the linear term in $E_{ex}$ induces
L000497	a distinct linear exciton dispersion near the BZ center, as illustrated
L000498	in Fig. \ref{fig:Schematic of Dimensionality effect}(d). When the
L000499	parabolic contributions arising from $E_{k}$ and $E_{d}$ are dominated
L000500	by a strong $E_{ex}$ term, the linear behavior of the exciton dispersion
L000501	persists over an extended range from the BZ center. This enhanced
L000502	linear regime becomes more accessible for experimental observation
L000503	through HREELS.
L000504	
L000505	Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8} is a Mott insulator with
L000506	relatively flat LHB and UHB. As a result, the kinetic term $E_{k}$
L000507	can be treated as a constant, independent of the momentum $\boldsymbol{q}$,
L000508	which is consistent with the observed flat dispersion of the IT {[}Fig.
L000509	\ref{fig:Non-Analytic Exciton Dispersion and Dimensionality effect}(c-f){]}.
L000510	The breathing Kagome lattice structure, which promotes significant
L000511	overlap of the electron-hole wavefunctions, further suppresses the
L000512	Coulomb screening \citep{RN639,RN634}. Consequently, Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000513	exhibits enhanced exchange interactions, i.e., $E_{ex}$ dominates
L000514	the exciton dynamics, providing the primary mechanism behind the observed
L000515	dimensional dependence of the exciton dispersions. The spontaneous
L000516	structural phase transition, which notably alters the interlayer coupling
L000517	strength, establishes Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8} as
L000518	an ideal natural platform for investigating excitonic dimensional
L000519	effects. In the $\alpha$ phase, the strong vdW nature of Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000520	results in negligible interlayer coupling, and thus excitons are confined
L000521	within the 2D layers, with the in-plane screening effect \citep{RN608,RN589,RN580}
L000522	predominantly contributing to the 2D massless linear exciton dispersion.
L000523	In contrast, in the $\beta$ phase, the strong interlayer hybridization
L000524	alters the electronic properties, causing the excitons to no longer
L000525	be localized within 2D layers. This leads to a more pronounced out-of-plane
L000526	screening effect, resulting in exciton dispersion that exhibits 3D
L000527	characteristics.
L000528	
L000529	In summary, we observed exciton splitting across the phase transition
L000530	of Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}, originating from bonding-antibonding
L000531	splitting due to enhanced interlayer coupling. More importantly, in
L000532	the $\alpha$ phase, we definitively demonstrate the presence of a
L000533	quasi-2D massless exciton dispersion, which transitions to a 3D parabolic
L000534	dispersion due to the significant enhancement of interlayer coupling
L000535	across the phase transition. This unique variation in interlayer coupling
L000536	strength makes Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8} an ideal platform
L000537	for studying the dimensional effects on excitonic band structures.
L000538	Beyond the qualitative similarities to 2D semiconductors, the correlated
L000539	nature of Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8} necessitates advanced
L000540	many-body treatments. We expect these results to catalyze future theoretical
L000541	and experimental efforts to clarify the unique excitonic mechanisms
L000542	in the correlated regime.

L000563	\emph{Principle of the 2D HREELS.} HREELS probes elementary excitations
L000564	via the inelastic scattering of a monochromatic electron beam \citep{raether2006excitation}.
L000565	In traditional HREELS measurements, which employ a fixed scattering
L000566	geometry (with fixed incident and scattering angles), an EDC is acquired
L000567	at a single momentum point. By analyzing the energy and angle of the
L000568	monochromatic electron beam before and after scattering, the energy
L000569	of the elementary excitation and the momentum parallel to the sample
L000570	surface can be determined based on the principles of energy and momentum
L000571	conservation {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Instrument}(a){]} \citep{RN650}:
L000572	
L000573	\begin{equation}
L000574	E_{Loss}=E_{i}-E_{s},
L000575	\end{equation}
L000576	\begin{equation}
L000577	q_{\parallel}=\frac{\sqrt{2mE_{i}}}{\hbar}\left(\sin\alpha_{i}-\sqrt{1-\frac{E_{Loss}}{E_{i}}}\sin\alpha_{s}\right).
L000578	\end{equation}
L000579	
L000580	\noindent where $E_{i}$ and $E_{s}$ are the energy of incident and
L000581	scattering electrons, in sequence. To acquire the dispersion of elementary
L000582	excitations, it is necessary to change the momentum points by rotating
L000583	the angles of the analyzer, sample, and monochromator.
L000584	
L000585	In contrast, our HREELS setup is equipped with a hemispherical energy
L000586	analyzer, enabling 2D mapping of momentum and energy simultaneously
L000587	without the need to rotate the sample or analyzer, significantly enhancing
L000588	data acquisition efficiency {[}Fig. \ref{fig:Instrument}(b){]}. Under
L000589	this instrumental configuration, the ultimate energy and momentum
L000590	resolutions can reach $0.7\ {\rm meV}$ and $0.002\ \text{\AA}^{-1}$,
L000591	respectively \citep{RN604}. In the present work, to optimize detection
L000592	efficiency and ensure a high signal-to-noise ratio for the observed
L000593	excitonic features, we utilized an operating energy resolution of
L000594	$3.0\ {\rm meV}$ and a momentum resolution of $0.005\ \text{\AA}^{-1}$.
L000595	\textit{In-situ} HREELS measurements in this study were performed
L000596	using a monochromatic electron beam with an incident angle of 60�
L000597	and an incident energy of 110 eV.
L000598	
L000599	\emph{Probing Depth of HREELS.} While HREELS is typically characterized
L000600	as a surface-sensitive technique, the effective probing depth depends
L000601	fundamentally on the underlying scattering mechanism. It is essential
L000602	to distinguish between impact scattering and dipole scattering. In
L000603	the impact scattering regime, the probing depth is governed by the
L000604	inelastic mean free path of the probe electrons---typically $5-10\ \lyxmathsym{\AA}$
L000605	for incident energies in the $50-100\ {\rm eV}$ range---rendering
L000606	the technique strictly sensitive to the topmost atomic layers.
L000607	
L000608	In contrast, the dipole scattering mechanism, which dominates the
L000609	excitonic measurements near the $\Gamma$ point in this study, involves
L000610	long-range electromagnetic interactions. In this regime, the probing
L000611	depth is independent of the inelastic mean free path. The HREELS cross-section
L000612	is directly proportional to the spectral function $S(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)$,
L000613	which describes the collective electronic response of the system \citep{RN12}:
L000614	
L000615	\[
L000616	S(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{0}S(\boldsymbol{q},z,z',\omega)e^{-|\boldsymbol{q}|\cdot|z+z'|}dzdz'
L000617	\]
L000618	
L000619	\noindent where $z$ and $z'$ are coordinates perpendicular to the
L000620	surface. The term $S(\boldsymbol{q},z,z',\omega)$ represents the
L000621	density-density correlation function:
L000622	
L000623	\begin{gather*}
L000624	S(\boldsymbol{q},z,z',\omega)=\sum_{m,n}\left[\langle m|\hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{z})|n\rangle\cdot\langle n|\hat{\rho}(-\boldsymbol{q},z')|m\rangle P_{m}\right]\\
L000625	\cdot\delta(E-E_{n}+E_{m})
L000626	\end{gather*}
L000627	
L000628	\noindent where $\hat{\rho}$ is the charge density operator, $P_{m}=e^{-E_{m}/k_{B}T}/Z$
L000629	is the Boltzmann factor, and $|m\rangle$, $|n\rangle$ denote the
L000630	many-body states of the sample with energies $E_{m}$ and $E_{n}$,
L000631	respectively.
L000632	
L000633	Crucially, the weighting factor $e^{-|\boldsymbol{q}|\cdot|z+z'|}$
L000634	in the integral dictates that the effective probing depth scales as
L000635	$\sim1/|\boldsymbol{q}|$. Within our investigated momentum range
L000636	($0.00$ to $0.06\ \text{\AA}^{-1}$), the probing depth extends significantly
L000637	beneath the surface, thereby encompassing multiple van der Waals layers.
L000638	Consequently, the excitonic signals detected in Nb\textsubscript{3}Cl\textsubscript{8}
L000639	originate from the collective response of many near-surface layers,
L000640	effectively representing the intrinsic bulk-like properties of the
L000641	material. This ensures that the observed evolution of exciton dispersion
L000642	is a manifestation of dimensionality-driven effects rather than a
L000643	localized surface phenomenon.
